questionText: In how many ways can the number 98 be expressed as a product of two numbers?
hints: Writing a number as a product of two numbers means finding its factor pairs. Each pair counts once, whichever way round it is written.
Start with 1 × 98. Then test 2, 3, 4 and so on to see which of them divide 98 exactly, and write each one with its partner.
Here is a similar one: 30 can be written as 1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10 and 5 × 6. There are no other pairs, so 30 can be written as a product of two numbers in 4 ways.

stepByStep.text: Every number has the pair made with 1, so the first way is 1 × 98.
98 is even, so 2 divides it.
3, 4, 5 and 6 do not divide 98 exactly, but 7 does.
The next factors of 98 are 14 and 49, and they have been used already, so there are no new pairs.
98 can be expressed as a product of two numbers in 3 ways: 1 × 98, 2 × 49 and 7 × 14.

misconceptions.A: 1 way counts only 1 × 98. Test 2 and 7 as well, because both divide 98 exactly.
misconceptions.B: 2 ways is one pair short. Besides 1 × 98 and 2 × 49, there is also 7 × 14.
misconceptions.C: Great job! The pairs are 1 × 98, 2 × 49 and 7 × 14.
misconceptions.D: 6 is the number of factors of 98. Each product uses two factors, so the six factors make three pairs.

questionText: A typist types all the Prime Numbers between 1 to 100. How many times did she press the number key having 2 on it?
hints: Two ideas are mixed here: which numbers are prime, and which digits they are written with. Only the prime numbers get typed.
A 2 can appear in the ones place or in the tens place. Think about which prime numbers can end in 2, and then look for primes among the numbers from 20 to 29.
Here is a similar one for the 6 key. No prime ends in 6, because a number ending in 6 is even. From 60 to 69 the only primes are 61 and 67. So the 6 key is pressed 2 times.

stepByStep.text: A number ending in 2 is even, so the only prime ending in 2 is 2 itself. That is one press.
Now look at 20 to 29, where 2 is in the tens place. The even numbers there are not prime, and neither are 21, 25 and 27, because 21 = 3 × 7, 25 = 5 × 5 and 27 = 3 × 9.
That leaves 23 and 29, which are both prime. Each one needs one press of the 2 key.
The primes with a 2 in them are 2, 23 and 29, so she pressed the 2 key 3 times. The trap is counting numbers such as 12, 22 or 32, which have a 2 but are not prime.

misconceptions.A: 1 counts only the prime number 2. Look also at the numbers from 20 to 29, where 2 is the tens digit, and find the primes there.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! Only 2, 23 and 29 are primes with a 2 in them.
misconceptions.C: 7 is too many. This can happen when numbers such as 21, 25 or 27 are counted, but each of them can be divided by a smaller number.
misconceptions.D: 19 is how many numbers from 1 to 100 have a 2 in them. Only the prime numbers are typed, so check which of those are prime.

questionText: The three digit numbers, 5 ★ 7, 5 7 ♥ and Ψ 5 9 are all divisible by 11. What is the greatest number formed by the values of ★, ♥ and Ψ?
hints: This uses the test for dividing by 11. Each symbol hides one digit, and the test lets you find it.
For a three-digit number, add the first and last digits and subtract the middle digit. If the result is 0 or 11, the number can be divided by 11. Try this on 5 ★ 7 first.

Here is a similar one: the number 6 □ 9 can be divided by 11. The first and last digits add up to 15, and 15 less the middle digit must be 0 or 11. So the middle digit is 4 and the number is 649, which is 11 × 59.

stepByStep.text: The test for 11: in a three-digit number, the first digit plus the last digit, less the middle digit, must come to 0 or 11.
In 5 ★ 7 the first and last digits add up to 12, so ★ must be 1 to leave 11. The number is 517.
In 5 7 ♥ the middle digit is 7, so 5 plus ♥ must equal 7 to leave 0. That makes ♥ equal to 2, and the number is 572.
In Ψ 5 9, Ψ plus 9 less 5 must come to 11. That makes Ψ equal to 7, and the number is 759.
The hidden digits are 1, 2 and 7. Putting the biggest digit first gives the greatest number, 721.

misconceptions.A: 723 uses a 3, but the hidden digits are 1, 2 and 7. Check ★ again: 5 + 7 less ★ must leave 11.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The hidden digits are 1, 2 and 7, and the greatest number they make is 721.
misconceptions.C: 972 uses a 9, but 9 is a digit printed in the question and not one of the hidden digits. Find ★, ♥ and Ψ with the test for 11.
misconceptions.D: 729 uses a 9, but 9 is a digit printed in the question and not one of the hidden digits. Find ★, ♥ and Ψ with the test for 11.

questionText: The H.C.F. of 65 and 91 is:
hints: H.C.F. means the highest common factor, the biggest number that divides both numbers exactly. Neither number here is in the easy times tables, so break them into prime factors.
Break 65 into prime factors. It ends in 5, so divide by 5 first. Then test whether the other prime factor also divides 91.
Here is a similar one: for the HCF of 38 and 57, write 38 = 2 × 19 and 57 = 3 × 19. Both share 19, so the HCF is 19.

stepByStep.text: 65 ends in 5, so divide it by 5. Its prime factors are 5 and 13.
91 does not end in 0 or 5, so 5 does not divide it. Try 13, and it divides 91 exactly.
Both numbers share the factor 13 and nothing bigger, so the H.C.F. of 65 and 91 is 13.

misconceptions.A: 17 does not divide 65, because 17 × 3 = 51 and 17 × 4 = 68. Break 65 into 5 × 13 and test those factors on 91.
misconceptions.B: 1 divides every number, but there is a bigger common factor here. 91 looks prime, yet it is 7 × 13.
misconceptions.C: You got it! 65 = 5 × 13 and 91 = 7 × 13, so the H.C.F. is 13.
misconceptions.D: 15 does not divide 65, because 15 × 4 = 60 and 15 × 5 = 75. Break 65 into 5 × 13 and test those factors on 91.

questionText: The L.C.M. of which two numbers is the greatest?
hints: The L.C.M. is the smallest number that both numbers divide exactly. Every pair here has 15 in it, so find each L.C.M. and compare them; the pair with the biggest numbers does not always win.
For each pair, go through the multiples of 15, which are 15, 30, 45, 60, 75 and 90. Stop at the first one that the other number also divides.

Here is a similar one: which is greater, the LCM of 10 and 25 or the LCM of 10 and 12? The multiples of 10 are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60. 25 first divides 50, and 12 first divides 60. So 10 and 12 have the greater LCM, even though 12 is smaller than 25.

stepByStep.text: For 15 and 25, the first multiple of 15 that 25 divides is 75.
For 15 and 20, the first multiple of 15 that 20 divides is 60.
For 15 and 18, none of 30, 45, 60 and 75 can be divided by 18, but 90 can.
For 15 and 12, the first multiple of 15 that 12 divides is 60.
The greatest L.C.M. is 90, which belongs to 15 & 18. The trap is that 25 is the biggest partner, but it shares the factor 5 with 15, and that keeps its L.C.M. down to 75.

misconceptions.A: 25 is the biggest partner, but the L.C.M. of 15 and 25 is only 75 because they share the factor 5. Work out the L.C.M. of every pair before choosing.
misconceptions.B: The L.C.M. of 15 and 20 is 60, and another pair reaches higher. Work out the L.C.M. of every pair before choosing.
misconceptions.C: Great job! The L.C.M. of 15 and 18 is 90, the greatest of the four.
misconceptions.D: The L.C.M. of 15 and 12 is 60, and another pair reaches higher. Work out the L.C.M. of every pair before choosing.

questionText: How many factors does 84 have?
hints: Factors are the numbers that divide a number exactly. They come in pairs that multiply to give the number, so listing the pairs in order helps you miss none.
Start with 1 × 84 and 2 × 42. Carry on testing 3, 4, 5, 6 and so on, writing each factor with its partner.
Here is a similar one: the factor pairs of 100 are 1 × 100, 2 × 50, 4 × 25, 5 × 20 and 10 × 10. The last pair uses 10 twice, so it adds only one factor, and 100 has 9 factors.

stepByStep.text: List the factor pairs in order. The first four are 1 × 84, 2 × 42, 3 × 28 and 4 × 21.
5 does not divide 84 exactly. The next pairs are 6 × 14 and 7 × 12.
8 and 9 do not divide 84 exactly, and the next factor is 12, which is already in the list. So every pair has been found.
There are 6 pairs, and each pair gives 2 factors.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 84 has six factor pairs, which makes 12 factors.
misconceptions.B: 8 factors is too few, so some pairs are missing. Go through 1 to 9 in order and check 3 × 28, 4 × 21, 6 × 14 and 7 × 12.
misconceptions.C: 10 factors is one pair short. Go through 1 to 9 in order and make sure 4 × 21 and 6 × 14 are both on your list.
misconceptions.D: 14 factors is too many. Check each number you listed by dividing; 5, 8 and 9 do not divide 84 exactly.

questionText: Which of the following is not the sum of two prime numbers?
hints: Prime numbers have exactly two factors; the first few are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11. Test each number to see whether two primes can add up to it.

Remember that 2 is a prime, and it is the only even prime. Two odd numbers always add up to an even number, so an odd total needs the prime 2 as one part. For each odd number, take 2 away and see whether what is left is prime.
Here is a similar one. Is 9 the sum of two primes? 9 − 2 = 7, and 7 is prime, so 9 = 2 + 7. Is 17? 17 − 2 = 15, and 15 = 3 × 5 is not prime, so 17 is not the sum of two primes.

stepByStep.text: 5 is the sum of the primes 2 and 3.
7 is the sum of the primes 2 and 5.
12 is the sum of the primes 5 and 7.
11 is odd, so one of its two primes would have to be 2, the only even prime. That leaves 9, and 9 is 3 × 3, so it is not prime.
So 11 is not the sum of two prime numbers. The trap is that 11 is a prime itself, but that does not make it a sum of two primes.

misconceptions.A: 5 is 2 + 3, and both 2 and 3 are prime. Remember that 2 counts as a prime number.
misconceptions.B: 7 is 2 + 5, and both 2 and 5 are prime. Remember that 2 counts as a prime number.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! An odd total needs the prime 2, and 11 − 2 leaves 9, which is not prime.
misconceptions.D: 12 is 5 + 7, and both 5 and 7 are prime. Look for the number that cannot be split into two primes at all.

questionText: Ajay rolls three six-sided dice. The product of the three numbers is 90. What is the sum of the three numbers?
hints: Each die shows a number from 1 to 6. You need three such numbers that multiply to the given product, and breaking the product into prime factors shows which numbers are possible.
Break 90 into prime factors. Then look for a prime factor that cannot be joined with any other and still fit on a die.
Here is a similar one: three dice have a product of 75, and 75 = 3 × 5 × 5. No die shows 15 or 25, so the dice must show 3, 5 and 5. Their sum is 3 + 5 + 5 = 13.

stepByStep.text: Break 90 into prime factors.
A die has no 10 or 15, so the 5 must be on a die by itself. The other two dice then multiply to 18.
Using numbers from 1 to 6, 18 can only be made as 3 × 6, because 2 × 9 would need a 9.
So the dice show 3, 5 and 6. There is only one possible set, so the sum can be found.
The sum of the three numbers is 14.

misconceptions.A: You got it! The dice must show 3, 5 and 6, and 3 + 5 + 6 = 14.
misconceptions.B: 18 is the product of the other two dice once the 5 is set aside. Find those two numbers, then add all three dice.
misconceptions.C: 10 is 2 + 3 + 5, the different prime factors of 90, but 2 × 3 × 5 is only 30. The three dice must multiply to 90.
misconceptions.D: It may seem that several sets of numbers could give 90, but with only 1 to 6 on a die, just 3, 5 and 6 fit. So the sum can be found.

questionText: What smallest number should be added to the product of 267 × 348 to make it divisible by 5?
hints: A number can be divided by 5 exactly only when its last digit is 0 or 5. So you only need the last digit of the product, not the whole product.
Find the last digit of 267 × 348 by multiplying just the ones digits, 7 and 8. Then ask how far that last digit is from the next 0 or 5.

Example: what smallest number should be added to 24 × 32 to make it divisible by 5? The ones digits give 4 × 2 = 8, so the product ends in 8. The next ending that works is 0, so add 2. Check: 24 × 32 = 768, and 768 + 2 = 770.

stepByStep.text: A number is divisible by 5 only when it ends in 0 or 5. So we only need the last digit of 267 × 348.
The last digit of a product comes from the ones digits. 7 × 8 = 56, so the product ends in 6.
After a number ending in 6, the next number that ends in 0 or 5 ends in 0. That is 4 more, because 6 + 4 = 10.
Check: 267 × 348 = 92,916, and 92,916 + 4 = 92,920, which ends in 0. The smallest number to add is 4.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The product ends in 6, and adding 4 makes it end in 0, so it can be divided by 5.
misconceptions.B: Adding 5 does not help here. The product ends in 6, so adding 5 makes it end in 1. Look at how far 6 is from the next 0.
misconceptions.C: Adding 7 would work only if the product ended in 3 or 8. Multiply the ones digits, 7 × 8, again to find the real last digit.
misconceptions.D: One of the numbers given does work. Find the last digit of the product from 7 × 8 and count up to the next number ending in 0.

questionText: The L.C.M. of 48 and 54 is:
hints: The L.C.M. is the smallest number that both numbers divide into exactly. It helps to break each number into a multiplication first.
Find the biggest number that divides both 48 and 54. Then write each number as that common number times something.
Example: for the L.C.M. of 12 and 18, the biggest number dividing both is 6. So 12 = 6 × 2 and 18 = 6 × 3. The L.C.M. is 6 × 2 × 3 = 36. Check: 36 ÷ 12 = 3 and 36 ÷ 18 = 2.

stepByStep.text: The biggest number that divides both 48 and 54 is 6. So 48 = 6 × 8 and 54 = 6 × 9.
The leftover parts, 8 and 9, share no factor except 1. So the L.C.M. is the common part once, times 8, times 9.
Check: 432 ÷ 48 = 9 and 432 ÷ 54 = 8, both exact. The L.C.M. of 48 and 54 is 432.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 432 is the smallest number that both 48 and 54 divide exactly.
misconceptions.B: 216 is 54 × 4, so 54 divides it, but 48 does not. The L.C.M. must be divisible by both numbers.
misconceptions.C: 480 is 48 × 10, so 48 divides it, but 54 does not. The L.C.M. must be divisible by both numbers.
misconceptions.D: 540 is 54 × 10, so 54 divides it, but 48 does not. The L.C.M. must be a multiple of both numbers.

questionText: Mrs. Geeta has two pieces of ribbons. One piece of ribbon is 84 meters long and the other is 108 meters long. She wants to cut the two ribbons into pieces of equal length with no ribbon left over. What is the greatest possible length of each piece of ribbon?
hints: Each piece must fit an exact number of times into both ribbons. So you are looking for the greatest number that divides both lengths, which is the H.C.F.
List the factors of 84, the shorter ribbon. Then see which of them also divide 108.
Example: ribbons of 30 metres and 45 metres. The factors of 30 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30. The largest one that also divides 45 is 15, so each piece is 15 metres long.

stepByStep.text: The piece length must divide both 84 and 108 exactly, with nothing left over. The greatest such length is the H.C.F. of 84 and 108.
Try the big ones on 108. 84, 42, 28, 21 and 14 do not divide 108, but 12 does, because 108 ÷ 12 = 9.
Also 84 ÷ 12 = 7. The greatest possible length of each piece is 12 metres.

misconceptions.A: 6 does divide both 84 and 108, but it is not the greatest length that does. Try a larger number that divides both.
misconceptions.B: 14 divides 84, because 14 × 6 = 84, but it does not divide 108. The piece length must divide both ribbons exactly.
misconceptions.C: Great work! 12 goes into 84 seven times and into 108 nine times, and no bigger length fits both.
misconceptions.D: 18 divides 108, because 18 × 6 = 108, but it does not divide 84. The piece length must divide both ribbons exactly.

questionText: How many factors does 30 have?
hints: Factors come in pairs that multiply to give the number. Listing the pairs in order makes sure none is missed.
Start with 1 × 30. Then try 2, 3, 4 and 5 in turn, and write down each pair that multiplies to 30.
Example: the factors of 28. The pairs are 1 × 28, 2 × 14 and 4 × 7. That is 3 pairs, so 28 has 6 factors.

stepByStep.text: Write 30 as a product of two numbers in every possible way: 1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10 and 5 × 6.
4 does not divide 30, and after 5 × 6 the pairs would only repeat. So the list is complete.
Each pair gives 2 factors: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30. There are 4 pairs, so 30 has 8 factors.

misconceptions.A: It looks as if one pair was missed. The pairs are 1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10 and 5 × 6, so count the factors again.
misconceptions.B: 4 is the number of pairs, not the number of factors. Each pair has two factors in it, so count both numbers of every pair.
misconceptions.C: 10 is one of the factors of 30, but the question asks how many factors there are. List them all and count them.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The factors are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30, which makes 8 of them.

questionText: A four digit number 8 ★ 2 ★ is divisible by 9, a same digit is represented by ★. Find the digit represented by ★?
hints: A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. Use that rule on the digits you know and the two missing ones.
Add the digits you can see, 8 and 2. The two stars are the same digit, so together they add twice that digit to the sum.
Example: 5 ★ 3 ★ is divisible by 9. The known digits give 5 + 3 = 8. The next multiple of 9 is 18, so the two stars must add 10, and each star is 5. Check: 5 + 5 + 3 + 5 = 18.

stepByStep.text: A number is divisible by 9 when its digits add up to a multiple of 9. The known digits add up to 8 + 2 = 10.
The next multiples of 9 after 10 are 18 and 27. So the two stars together must add 8 or 17.
The two stars are the same digit, so their total is an even number. That rules out 17, and 8 ÷ 2 = 4.
Check: 8 + 4 + 2 + 4 = 18, and 8,424 ÷ 9 = 936. The digit represented by ★ is 4.

misconceptions.A: 8 is what the two stars add up to together, not the value of one star. Share it equally between the two stars.
misconceptions.B: Well done! With 4 in both places the digits add up to 18, which is a multiple of 9.
misconceptions.C: With 5 in both places the digits add up to 8 + 5 + 2 + 5 = 20, and 20 is not a multiple of 9. Aim for a digit sum of 18.
misconceptions.D: With 3 in both places the digits add up to 8 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 16, and 16 is not a multiple of 9. Aim for a digit sum of 18.

questionText: What is the sum of the L.C.M. and H.C.F. of the numbers 24 and 32?
hints: This question has two parts. Find the H.C.F. and the L.C.M. of the two numbers separately, and then add them.
Start with the H.C.F. List the factors of 24 and pick the largest one that also divides 32.
Example: for 12 and 18, the H.C.F. is 6. The multiples of 18 are 18, 36, and 36 is also a multiple of 12, so the L.C.M. is 36. The sum is 36 + 6 = 42.

stepByStep.text: The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24. The largest one that also divides 32 is 8, so the H.C.F. is 8.
For the L.C.M., list the multiples of 32: 32, 64, 96. The first one that 24 also divides is 96, because 24 × 4 = 96.
Add the two: 96 + 8 = 104. The sum of the L.C.M. and H.C.F. is 104.

misconceptions.A: 96 is the L.C.M. on its own. The question asks for the sum, so the H.C.F. still has to be added.
misconceptions.B: Great job! The L.C.M. is 96 and the H.C.F. is 8, and 96 + 8 = 104.
misconceptions.C: It looks as if 4 was used as the H.C.F. A bigger number divides both 24 and 32, so look at the common factors again.
misconceptions.D: It looks as if 12 was used as the H.C.F. 12 divides 24 but not 32, so look for the largest number that divides both.

questionText: In writing all the prime numbers between 1 and 100, how many times would the digit 2 be used?
hints: Think about where a 2 could sit in a prime number below 100: in the ones place or in the tens place. Then remember what kind of numbers end in 2.
Any number ending in 2 is even, so check whether any prime at all can end in 2. After that, look at the numbers from 20 to 29 and pick out the primes.
Example: how many times is the digit 6 used in the primes up to 100? A number ending in 6 is even, so none of those is prime. In the sixties, only 61 and 67 are prime. So the digit 6 is used 2 times.

stepByStep.text: First look for a 2 in the ones place. Numbers ending in 2 are even, so 2 divides them. The only prime among them is 2 itself. That is one 2.
Now look for a 2 in the tens place, from 20 to 29. The even ones are out, and 21 = 3 × 7, 25 = 5 × 5 and 27 = 3 × 9. Only 23 and 29 are prime. That is two more.
The trap is to forget the prime 2 itself, or to count numbers like 12 and 22, which are not prime. The primes with a 2 are 2, 23 and 29, so the digit 2 is used 3 times.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The digit 2 appears in 2, 23 and 29, and in no other prime below 100.
misconceptions.B: One prime may have been missed. Count the 2 in 23, the 2 in 29, and also the prime number 2 itself.
misconceptions.C: 19 is how many numbers from 1 to 100 have a 2 in them. Only the prime numbers count here, so first pick out the primes that contain a 2.
misconceptions.D: Some primes do contain a 2. The number 2 is itself prime, and there are two more primes between 20 and 29.

questionText: Using all the one digit prime numbers form the greatest odd number?
hints: First decide which digits you may use: the prime numbers below 10. Then arrange them to make the biggest number that is still odd.
List the one-digit primes. An odd number must end in an odd digit, so think about which digit to keep for the ones place.
Example: the greatest odd number using 2, 4, 5 and 9. The ones digit must be odd. Keep the smaller odd digit, 5, for the ones place and write the rest biggest first: 9425.

stepByStep.text: The one-digit primes are 2, 3, 5 and 7. 9 is not prime, because 3 × 3 = 9.
For the greatest number put the biggest digits first: 7, then 5.
The number must be odd, so it cannot end in 2. Put 2 in the tens place and 3 in the ones place.
The greatest odd number is 7523.

misconceptions.A: 9 is not a prime number, because 3 × 3 = 9. Use only 2, 3, 5 and 7.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 7523 uses 2, 3, 5 and 7, starts with the biggest digits and ends in an odd digit.
misconceptions.C: This is odd and uses the right digits, but a bigger one can be made. Put 5 in the hundreds place.
misconceptions.D: This uses 9, which is not prime, and leaves out 2. The one-digit primes are 2, 3, 5 and 7.

questionText: Which two digits in the number 73251 should be interchanged so that it becomes completely divisible by 6?
hints: A number is divisible by 6 when it is divisible by both 2 and 3. Think about what swapping two digits changes and what it leaves the same.
Add the digits of 73251 to test for 3. Swapping digits does not change this sum, so then think about which digit must be in the ones place to make the number even.

Example: which two digits of 4,563 could be swapped to make it divisible by 6? The digits add up to 18, so 3 already divides it. It needs an even last digit. Swapping 6 and 3 gives 4,536, which is even, so it is divisible by 6.

stepByStep.text: To be divisible by 6, a number must be divisible by 3 and by 2. The digits of 73251 add up to 18, so 3 already divides it.
Swapping two digits never changes the digit sum, so the number stays divisible by 3. The key idea is that only the test for 2 matters now.
The number must end in an even digit. Its only even digit is 2, so the 2 must move to the ones place, where the 1 is now.
The swap gives 73152, and 73152 ÷ 6 = 12192. The digits to interchange are 2 & 1.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Moving the 2 to the end gives 73152, which is even and has a digit sum of 18.
misconceptions.B: Swapping 5 and 1 gives 73215, which ends in 5 and is odd. A number divisible by 6 must be even, so think about which digit has to go last.
misconceptions.C: Swapping 2 and 5 gives 73521, which still ends in 1 and is odd. The even digit has to move to the ones place.
misconceptions.D: Swapping 3 and 2 gives 72351, which still ends in 1 and is odd. The even digit has to move to the ones place.

questionText: A four digit number 9 ★ 8 ★, is divisible by 9, and ★ represents a same digit. Find the digit at the ★ place.
hints: The test for 9 uses the sum of the digits: it must be a multiple of 9. Remember that the same missing digit is used twice.
Add the digits you know, 9 and 8. Then find which multiple of 9 the total can reach when the same digit is added twice.
Example: 7 ★ 5 ★ is divisible by 9. The known digits give 7 + 5 = 12. The next multiple of 9 is 18, so the two stars add 6 and each star is 3. Check: 7 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 18.

stepByStep.text: A number is divisible by 9 when its digits add up to a multiple of 9. The known digits add up to 9 + 8 = 17.
The next multiples of 9 after 17 are 18, 27 and 36. So the two stars together must add 1, 10 or 19.
The two stars are the same digit, so their total is an even number. Only 10 fits, and 10 ÷ 2 = 5.
Check: 9 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 27, and 9,585 ÷ 9 = 1,065. The digit at the ★ place is 5.

misconceptions.A: Well done! With 5 in both places the digits add up to 27, which is a multiple of 9.
misconceptions.B: With 4 in both places the digits add up to 9 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 25, and 25 is not a multiple of 9. Aim for a digit sum of 27.
misconceptions.C: With 3 in both places the digits add up to 9 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 23, and 23 is not a multiple of 9. Aim for a digit sum of 27.
misconceptions.D: Adding 1 once to 17 would give 18, but the star appears twice. With 1 in both places the digits add up to 19, which is not a multiple of 9.

questionText: In how many ways can the number 136 be written as the product of two numbers?
hints: Each way of writing a number as a product of two numbers is a factor pair. So this is really a question about finding all the factor pairs.
Start with 1 × 136, then test 2, 3, 4 and so on. Each time a number divides 136 exactly, write down the pair.
Example: in how many ways can 50 be written as a product of two numbers? The pairs are 1 × 50, 2 × 25 and 5 × 10. That makes 3 ways.

stepByStep.text: Find every pair of numbers that multiply to 136. Start small: 1 × 136 and 2 × 68.
3 does not divide 136. 4 does, giving 4 × 34. Then 5, 6 and 7 do not, and 8 gives 8 × 17.
Going further only repeats the same pairs the other way round, such as 17 × 8. The trap is to count those again, or to leave out 1 × 136.
The pairs are 1 × 136, 2 × 68, 4 × 34 and 8 × 17. So 136 can be written as a product of two numbers in 4 ways.

misconceptions.A: 6 is more than the number of pairs. Check that a pair such as 8 × 17 and 17 × 8 was counted only once, since it is the same way.
misconceptions.B: One pair may have been missed. Remember that 1 × 136 counts, and so does 8 × 17.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The pairs are 1 × 136, 2 × 68, 4 × 34 and 8 × 17, which makes 4 ways.
misconceptions.D: There is one way too many here. List the pairs in order starting from 1 × 136 and check that each one really multiplies to 136.

questionText: Ajay writes all the multiples of 4 upto 100 and Vijay writes all the multiples of 5 upto 100, in their notebooks. How many common numbers could you find in both their notebooks?
hints: A number in both notebooks is a multiple of 4 and also a multiple of 5. Such numbers are the common multiples of the two.
Find the smallest number that is a multiple of both 4 and 5. Every common number is a multiple of that one.
Example: multiples of 3 and multiples of 4 up to 50. The smallest common multiple is 12. The multiples of 12 up to 50 are 12, 24, 36 and 48, so there are 4 common numbers.

stepByStep.text: A number in both notebooks must be a multiple of 4 and of 5. The smallest such number is 20.
Every common number is a multiple of 20. Up to 100 these are 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100.
Counting them, or working out 100 ÷ 20, gives 5. There are 5 common numbers in both notebooks.

misconceptions.A: 15 is too many. The shared numbers must be multiples of both 4 and 5, so list the multiples of 20 up to 100 and count them.
misconceptions.B: Great job! The common numbers are 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100, which makes 5.

questionText: The HCF of 39 and 65 is:
hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly. Breaking each number into a multiplication helps you see what they share.
Write 39 as a product of two smaller numbers. Then check whether either of those numbers divides 65.

questionText: Is 8,294 divisible by 11?
hints: There is a test for 11 that uses the digits in turn. You add every other digit to make two totals, and then compare the two totals.

questionText: Find the HCF of 30 and 36.
hints: The HCF is the biggest number that divides both numbers exactly.

questionText: Find the LCM of 6 and 9.
hints: The LCM is the smallest number that is in both times tables.
Write out the multiples of the bigger number, 9. After each one, ask: does 6 divide it exactly?
Example: LCM of 4 and 10. The multiples of 10 are 10, 20 and so on. 4 does not divide 10, but 4 divides 20. So the LCM is 20.

stepByStep.text: List the multiples of the bigger number, 9: 9, 18.
Look for the first one that 6 also divides. 6 does not divide 9 exactly, but 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
The LCM is 18.
